To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have used quantitative proteomics to identify population-specific biochemical networks of renal function in the marine and freshwater three spined stickleback.
we identified 120 proteins with population-specific abundance differences in the renal proteome of marine and freshwater sticklebacks.

the proteomes of kidneys of marine and fresh water (FW) sticklebacks have distinct biochemical networks that support the synthesis of organic osmolytes, and that the proteome of FW sticklebacks kidneys contains a high abundance of proteins that promote proteolysis, cell motility and calcium signaling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of the proteome of marine and freshwater stickleback kidneys.
the biochemical diversification of kidneys in sticklebacks, which is the first study of this kind in a vertebrate.
the biochemical basis for osmoregulation in marine and freshwater three spined sticklebacks, Gasterosteus aculeatus, a model species for evolutionary and ecological studies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
marine and freshwater sticklebacks have different renal proteomes, which are consistent with their different osmoregulatory requirements.
freshwater stickleback kidneys are more metabolically active, while the marine kidney is more focused on osmotic regulation.
freshwater sticklebacks have evolved an alternative strategy to cope with the osmotic challenge of freshwater, which involves the synthesis of organic osmolytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the marine stickleback kidney is more biochemically integrated than its freshwater counterpart, and that the marine kidney is specialized in the production of organic osmolytes, while the freshwater kidney is specialized in protein degradation, cytoskeletal remodeling and extracellular matrix remodeling.

the marine sticklebacks have higher levels of proteins involved in the production of organic osmolytes, whereas the freshwater sticklebacks have more proteins involved in proteolysis, cytoskeleton, extracellular matrix and calcium signalling.

freshwater and marine sticklebacks have different proteomes in their kidneys, which is likely to be due to the differences in their environment and the different functions of their kidneys in each environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the biochemical network that controls renal function in marine stickleback is more tightly controlled and has more proteins that are elevated than that of freshwater sticklebacks.
the kidney proteome is a rich source of information about the biochemical adaptations that enable marine and freshwater fish to thrive in their respective environments.
marine sticklebacks have a higher degree of synchronized abundance control than their freshwater counterparts, which is likely due to their more specialized physiology.
